item.title: Garment workers block highway in Gazipur, 50 factories declare holiday
item.description:
Garment workers blocked the Dhaka–Tangail highway in Gazipur and staged protests at around 9:30 am today, Tuesday, demanding that the minimum wage be raised to Tk 30,000. Protests by workers were reported in various parts of the district as well.

At around 9:30 am, workers took up positions on the Dhaka–Tangail highway in the Naojor area of Gazipur city. Many of them were seen carrying sticks. This brought traffic to a halt on that section of the highway, leaving passengers on long-distance buses and other vehicles stranded.

Garment workers clash with police in Mirpur

To avoid any untoward incidents amid the workers’ protests, the authorities declared a holiday today at 50 garment factories in various parts of the district. As a result, workers at these factories could not report for duty.

According to industrial police and local sources, at around 9:30 am, workers from Panasia Limited came out of their factory in the Naojor area of the city and took up positions on the western side of the highway flyover.

They then blocked the highway by putting up bamboo barricades. Traffic came to a halt on both sides of the highway. At the same time, workers from several factories in the Konabari, Mouchak and Telichala areas also stopped working and took to the streets.

Earlier, at around 9:45 am on Monday, workers had taken up positions on the highway in Naojor and staged protests by setting fires. Traffic was brought to a halt. During the protests that day, several police vehicles were set on fire. Workers also took to the streets and staged protests at various locations in the Konabari and Mouchak areas of the city.

No reports of road blockades like those seen in previous days came from the Chandra and Palli Bidyut areas of Kaliakair today. However, the situation there remained tense.

Amid the workers’ movement, members of law enforcement agencies were seen on alert at key points along various roads in the industrial area. Leaders and activists of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and its affiliated organisations also took up positions at several points.

How much should garment workers actually be paid?

Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Amzad Hossain said efforts were under way to persuade workers in the Naojor area to leave the road. He said protests by workers were continuing in some areas today as well. Law enforcement personnel were present in Naojor and were trying to persuade the workers to clear the road.

For several days, various industrial areas in Gazipur have witnessed protests, road blockades, vandalism and arson over the demand for a minimum wage of Tk 30,000. Several people, including police officers and journalists, have been injured in these incidents. Police vehicles, other vehicles and factory warehouses have also been set on fire.

item.title: Americans vote in midterms set to upend Trump presidency
item.description:
Americans deliver their verdict on Donald Trump's tumultuous second presidency Tuesday in midterm elections that threaten to shatter his grip on Washington, with Democrats poised to seize the House and challenge for control of the Senate.

Republicans losing the House would give Democrats the power to stall Trump's legislative agenda and launch sweeping investigations of his administration. A Senate defeat would also threaten his ability to appoint Supreme Court justices and senior officials.

The election amounts to a nationwide judgment on Trump, with the mood turning sharply against Republicans amid anger over soaring living costs and the war against Iran.

All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are at stake, along with governorships in 36 states. Democrats need only three House gains and a net four seats in the Senate to wrest both chambers from Republican hands.

Trump returned to office last year promising to bring down prices, but inflation, tariffs and fuel costs inflated by the Middle East conflict have squeezed Americans.

The 80-year-old's approval rating has hovered near the low 30s.

In the suburbs of Atlanta, Georgia, retired teacher Jane Callum, 77, was among Democrats canvassing for Senator Jon Ossoff who framed the race as a watershed moment for the country's future.

"I really feel an obligation to do everything that I possibly can to change the direction that our country is going in now, and put it more on the path to democracy and away from autocracy," she told AFP.

Democrats, Trump hold final rallies before midterm elections

Economic discontent

Republicans insist that Trump's tax cuts and immigration crackdown will benefit Americans and they are portraying Democratic candidates as left-wing radicals.

But in his final public campaign appearance Monday, Trump barely touched on the economy and spent most of the time in a rambling talk about his problem-plagued renovation of Washington's Reflecting Pool.

"This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime," he said, 26 minutes into the speech, before quickly returning to talking about renovations.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer branded it a "pathetic closing message."

Some Republican supporters remain confident.

"We're going to win. As a matter of fact, we've probably already won," Texas military veteran Yvonne Clouser told AFP.

But while Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, the battlefield is extending into conservative states like Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska.

Democrats must also defend competitive seats, including in Michigan, where a bitter internal dispute saw congresswoman Haley Stevens endorse Republican Mike Rogers rather than the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.

Decision Desk HQ's final forecast forecasted 241 House seats for Democrats against 194 for Republicans, and a narrower 52-48 Democratic Senate majority.

US strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island ahead of midterm elections

Disputed results?

Polls can underestimate one party's support, and Republicans hope their voters turn out in force on Election Day.

More than 57 million Americans had already voted early before Tuesday, indicating the high energy.

The campaign has attracted more than USD 11 billion in political advertising, while billionaire Trump ally Elon Musk has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican political efforts.

As soon as polls close, concerns will mount over whether results will be accepted by the Republicans.

Trump, who tried to overturn his 2020 election defeat, has repeatedly alleged widespread voter fraud and accused Democrats -- with no evidence -- of cheating.

The Justice Department, run by a close Trump ally, has already sued to potentially block certification of Alaska's Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses, although a court ruled against the effort on the eve of the election.

And the Supreme Court rejected on Monday an emergency bid to force California to set aside the mail-in ballots of more than 20,000 people on the grounds they may not be American citizens.

Trump, who will watch the midterms results at the White House on Tuesday night, signaled that if he does lose control of Congress he could simply defy Democrats.

"I veto everything," he told a podcast Monday, although he said he might strike deals with Democrats eventually.

item.title: US strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island ahead of midterm elections
item.description:
The United States on Monday attacked Iran's Qeshm Island, the Wall Street Journal reported, even as President Donald Trump signaled progress in negotiations with Tehran to end the eight-month-old conflict.

The Journal, citing unnamed US officials, described the strike against Qeshm, the the largest island in the Strait of Hormuz, as the latest of a series of limited strikes Washington has secretly carried out against Iran in recent weeks.

Democrats, Trump hold final rallies before midterm elections

Iranian state news agency IRNA reported five explosions in rapid succession were heard on the island, and that some residents reported seeing two aircraft flying in its skies.

The Pentagon referred questions about the reported strikes to US Central Command, which did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment late Monday.

The Journal reported that US has been engaged in smaller-scale strikes against Iran for several weeks.

The paper said the US has not publicly announced the attacks, so as not to signal any intention of resuming major combat operations.

It said some officials described the assaults as defensive in nature to prevent Iran from having the freedom to attack commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, a key conduit for oil shipments that has been largely blocked since the war began in late February.

Trump rules out new Iran attack before US midterm elections

On Monday, on the eve of midterm elections in the United States, Trump said that a deal with Tehran "could happen."

Oil prices, sent rocketing by Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz energy corridor, plunged by more than seven percent on Monday on optimism over a possible end to the conflict.

item.title: How much should garment workers actually be paid?
item.description:
Thousands of garment workers took to the streets. Clashes with police and incidents such as vehicles being set on fire unfolded within a short time. The workers are demanding a minimum wage of Tk 30,000.

Some have expressed irritation, asking whether workers have become too demanding—is Tk 30,000 something that can simply be handed out? Others want to know how reasonable the demand actually is.

The good news is that the government has announced the formation of a new wage board. However, there is a tendency to look for government conspiracies in everything, whether right or wrong. This time has been no exception.

The minimum wage was set at Tk 12,500 in December 2023. Since then, the cost of living has risen significantly due to war, inflation, gas shortages and other factors. According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics, inflation stood at 8.34 per cent in September 2026.

The wage growth rate was 8.05 per cent in August. In this way, inflation has consistently outpaced wage growth for nearly four and a half years since February 2022. In other words, the real income of working people has declined every month for the past four and a half years.

RMG workers clash with police in Ashulia amid protests, vehicle set on fire, 2 detained
If we use minimum fairness as the benchmark, the worker’s wage should be at least Tk 17,500 simply to maintain the previous level of real income—that is, to adjust for inflation. Second, to keep the shortfall from exceeding the previous Tk 3,000, the wage would need to be Tk 18,000.

Expenses have increased by 16.7 per cent, while wages have risen by 6.7 per cent. For every Tk 1 increase in wages, expenses have gone up by Tk 3. Where will the additional money come from?

Drawing on my earlier research on garment workers, I recently set out to examine the situation on the ground and update my understanding of their circumstances. In the process, I gained a fairly clear picture of a garment worker’s monthly expenses. In January 2026, a family of four was living on the earnings of a single worker.

At an average of Tk 4,500 per person, the family needed Tk 18,000 to cover basic necessities—expenses that were essential for survival. There was no luxury, no new spending and certainly no savings. Including overtime, the worker earned a total of Tk 15,000. The remaining Tk 3,000 had to be borrowed; otherwise, the family had to survive on mashed potatoes and lentils for the last 10 to 15 days of the month.

RMG workers block Dhaka–Narayanganj link road

My calculations show that by January 2027, the minimum amount needed for the family to survive will be Tk 21,000, based on an average of Tk 5,250 per person. The worker’s earnings, including the wage increase and overtime, will be no more than Tk 16,000.

That leaves a shortfall of Tk 5,000. The figures may vary slightly, but over the course of a year, the worker’s monthly debt will increase by an additional Tk 2,000 on top of the existing Tk 3,000.

Meanwhile, because of the depreciation of the taka, the real value of the worker’s Tk 16,000 income in January 2027, calculated at January 2026 prices, will be only Tk 13,714. In other words, although the wage has technically “increased” on paper, real income has fallen by nearly Tk 1,286, or 8.6 per cent.

If we use minimum fairness as the benchmark, the worker’s wage should be at least Tk 17,500 simply to maintain the previous level of real income—that is, to adjust for inflation. Second, to keep the shortfall from exceeding the previous Tk 3,000, the wage would need to be Tk 18,000.

Dhaka-Tangail highway blocked again by garment workers, BGB deployed

This means that the government, or the owners through government mediation, must somehow provide an additional Tk 2,000 in assistance on top of the Tk 16,000 wage. Otherwise, how will the worker survive? Third, if there is a genuine willingness to eliminate the shortfall entirely, the worker must be paid at least Tk 21,000.

Note that the Tk 2,000 in assistance is not a bonus; it is the minimum condition for keeping the family in the same debt-ridden position as before. Otherwise, the family will slide from poverty into extreme poverty, struggling to afford even one or two meals a day.

British sociologist Seebohm Rowntree first demonstrated that a minimum wage could be measured against a budget covering a family’s basic needs. This tradition gave rise to Richard and Martha Anker’s “living wage” methodology, which is now an internationally accepted and widely recognised standard.

According to the Global Living Wage Coalition’s 2025 estimates, the living wage for a worker in Dhaka, supporting a family of four in which an average of 1.58 members earn an income, is Tk 30,459 per month. The workers’ demand for Tk 30,000 almost exactly matches the figure in this international research.

In his book Poverty and Famines, Amartya Sen showed that the Bengal famine of 1943 was not caused by a shortage of food. It happened because people’s “entitlements” collapsed: the amount of rice they could buy with their wages suddenly fell.

Two.

According to the ILO’s Minimum Wage Fixing Convention, 1970 (No. 131), the needs of workers and their families, as well as the cost of living, must be taken into account when setting minimum wages. Automatically adjusting wages in line with the cost of living is an established practice in many countries.

In his book Poverty and Famines, Amartya Sen showed that the Bengal famine of 1943 was not caused by a shortage of food. It happened because people’s “entitlements” collapsed: the amount of rice they could buy with their wages suddenly fell.

Rice was available in the market, but workers could no longer afford it with their wages. A garment worker’s entitlement is their wage. When the ratio between wages and the price of rice declines, deprivation enters the household even when the markets are full.

Economics also offers an answer to the concern that “factories will not be able to operate if wages are raised too much”. The “efficiency wage” theory developed by economists George Akerlof, Carl Shapiro and Joseph Stiglitz holds that better wages increase workers’ productivity, reduce employee turnover and save on training costs.

Government forms new wage board to increase garment workers’ salaries

Economists David Card and Alan Krueger showed in New Jersey, in the United States, that raising the minimum wage did not reduce employment. Card received the Nobel Prize in 2021 for research in this field.

The government and factory owners have one question: who will pay for this?

The responsibility does not rest with factory owners alone; all three parties have a role. International buyer brands have kept garment prices under control for years. It is the responsibility of the government and factory owners to persuade them to ensure that workers’ wage costs are separately protected in the purchase price. Factory owners must also allocate a fair share of their profits to wages.

The state, meanwhile, must arrange to cover part of the shortfall through rationing, subsidised essential goods, housing and transport assistance. Amartya Sen and Jean Drèze have called this “public action”. When the market cannot keep people alive, the state must take responsibility.

The concerns of factory owners are also valid. There are shortages of gas and electricity. Tensions in the Middle East have made the fuel market uncertain. Buyers do not want to raise prices. Competition with Vietnam and Cambodia is intense. If wages are suddenly doubled, smaller factories may shut down, putting workers at risk of losing their jobs and suffering further hardship.

In pictures: Police use tear gas, water cannons as garment workers clash in Mirpur

But if one reality is emphasised while another is ignored, disaster is inevitable. Real incomes have declined for four and a half consecutive years. The living wage under international standards is Tk 30,459, while the minimum wage has remained stuck at Tk 12,500 for nearly three years.

Workers taking to the streets are therefore not demanding extravagant benefits; they are seeking the minimum assurance needed to survive. Understanding this with empathy will point the way to a solution.

Of the country’s export earnings of USD 48 billion in fiscal year 2025–26, USD 38 billion, or approximately 80.6 per cent, came from the garment sector. Bangladesh is the world’s second-largest garment exporter after China.

The workforce taking to the streets is the very force behind the dollars needed for imports, foreign exchange reserves and the exchange rate. It is economically flawed and unjust to expect the families of those who generate 80 per cent of the country’s export earnings to survive on debt.

*Helal Mohiuddin is a faculty member in Liberal Arts at Mayville State University, North Dakota, USA.

*The views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Prothom Alo to celebrate anniversary tomorrow with a range of programmes
item.description:
Prothom Alo is preparing to celebrate its anniversary with a festive atmosphere and a range of activities. Preparations are under way for special supplements, a redesigned app, various programmes organised by the Bondhushava, and a reunion for employees.

The entire Prothom Alo family is busy making arrangements for the celebrations. Tomorrow, 4 November, marks the 28th anniversary of Prothom Alo.

The newspaper has taken several initiatives for its readers, well-wishers and employees to mark the occasion.

With the motto “ja kichu bhalo, tar shonge Prothom Alo (Prothom Alo stands with everything that is good)”, the newspaper published its first edition on 4 November 1998.

With its crisp printing, colourful photographs, 12-page format, new feature pages every day, commitment to political neutrality, practice of objective journalism, professional excellence and continuous efforts to embrace new ideas, Prothom Alo became an indispensable companion for the people of Bangladesh. It became a member of their families.

Within just a few years, Prothom Alo earned recognition as the country's most widely circulated daily newspaper.

Overcoming various challenges and adversities, it has evolved into more than just a newspaper, becoming a digital platform as well, while remaining committed to truth and facts. Beyond Bangladesh, Prothom Alo has received a warm welcome from Bengali-speaking readers around the world.

It has also earned prestigious recognition from international organisations such as WAN-IFRA and INMA, receiving awards as one of the world's and Asia's best media outlets.

To mark the anniversary, special supplements will accompany the main newspaper on four days.

The supplements, scheduled for publication on 4, 6, 8 and 10 November, will explore various aspects of the country's people and society, the relationship between citizens and the state, the perspectives of the younger generation, and questions and analyses concerning the future of Bangladesh.

Over these four days, the main newspaper and its supplements will together comprise 32 to 36 pages.

The special supplements will seek to explore a range of questions: what life is like for people in different parts of the country, whether in the capital, rural areas, river islands or the hills; what debates are taking place over the relationship between citizens and the state; where Gen Z finds meaning in life; and what Bangladesh's future might look like.

Prominent writers from across the country will contribute articles, while interviews with experts from various sectors will also feature. Details of the supplements have been published in an advertisement on the back page of today's Prothom Alo.

On 4 November, the anniversary itself, Prothom Alo will launch a redesigned version of its app. The updated app will introduce several new features to provide readers with an easier and more convenient experience. Its design and navigation system will also undergo changes.

As in previous years, Prothom Alo has organised a reunion for its employees to mark the anniversary. The event will take place at a venue in the capital on 4 November.

Prothom Alo representatives working in Dhaka and across the country will attend. Discussions at the event will cover the newspaper's future plans, new ideas and various aspects of the media industry.

Yesterday, Monday, the organisation held an online preparatory meeting involving employees from Dhaka and other parts of the country.

Prothom Alo Bondhushava has also arranged various programmes across the country to mark the anniversary. These include a range of public welfare and cultural activities. Through these initiatives, the organisation aims to strengthen its engagement with local communities.

item.title: Clashes erupt in Mirpur for third consecutive day
item.description:
Clashes between police and garment workers erupted in Mirpur for the third consecutive day on Tuesday, disrupting traffic and prompting the temporary closure of Mirpur-11 metro station.
The clashes began around 10:15am when police intervened to prevent workers from blocking the road in the Mirpur-11 area, eyewitnesses said.
Workers intermittently emerged from side streets and hurled bricks and stones at police, who responded by firing tear gas shells and sound grenades to disperse them. The confrontation triggered repeated chases and counter-chases, leaving the area tense and traffic at a standstill.
Earlier in the morning, garment workers had left their factories and gathered outside their workplaces, with groups assembling along nearby side streets.
Yusuf Ahmed, a local resident and eyewitness, told Bangla Tribune that male and female workers from several factories between Mirpur-10 and Mirpur-11 had gathered outside their workplaces.
“Looking at the situation, it seems they could take to the main road at any moment,” he said.
Police remained on high alert as the situation developed.
Hafizur Rahman, officer-in-charge of Mirpur police station, said the situation in Mirpur-10 was normal.
“We remain on high alert, and any attempt to cause disorder will be met with strict action,” he said.
Garment workers have been protesting for some time, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000. The protests turned violent on Sunday, when workers set fire to a police vehicle and clashed with law enforcement personnel.
Workers attempted to take to the streets again on Monday but were prevented from doing so by police.
According to a police source, around six people were arrested on Monday in connection with the unrest. Eleven cases have been filed over the clashes of the past two days, with more than 10,000 people named as accused.

item.title: Jail Killing Day: Bangladesh remembers four national leaders
item.description:
November 3 is observed as Jail Killing Day, marking the assassination of four prominent national leaders inside Dhaka Central Jail on this day in 1975.
The victims were Syed Nazrul Islam, acting president of the wartime Mujibnagar government; Tajuddin Ahmad, the country’s first prime minister; and cabinet members Captain M Mansur Ali and AHM Qamaruzzaman.
The killings took place less than three months after the assassination of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and most of his family members on August 15, 1975. The four leaders, close associates of Bangabandhu and key figures in the Liberation War, had been arrested and imprisoned following the coup.
On November 4, 1975, Kazi Abdul Awal, then deputy inspector general of prisons, filed a murder case at Lalbagh police station over the killings. The case subsequently became known as the Jail Killing Case.
Investigations remained stalled for 21 years. Legal proceedings resumed after the Awami League returned to power in June 1996.
On October 20, 2004, the Dhaka Metropolitan Sessions Judge’s Court delivered its verdict, sentencing eight people to life imprisonment and three to death.
Of the 11 convicts, 10 remain fugitives, while one death sentence has been carried out. Captain (dismissed) Abdul Majed, who was sentenced to life imprisonment in the Jail Killing Case, had also been sentenced to death in the Bangabandhu assassination case.
Majed, who had remained a fugitive for years, was arrested after returning to Bangladesh in April 2020. He was executed later that month.

item.title: Workers block Dhaka-Tangail highway, set fire to roadside waste in Gazipur
item.description:
Garment workers blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur’s Naojor area on Tuesday, setting fire to roadside waste and bringing traffic to a standstill.
The blockade began around 9:30am in front of Diganta Sweater factory.
Workers dragged accumulated rubbish and waste from the roadside onto the highway and set it on fire, disrupting traffic between Joydebpur Chourasta and Naojor intersection.
Protesters also obstructed all vehicles, including auto-rickshaws and motorcycles. Some were seen playing cricket on the highway.
Journalists at the scene faced resistance from protesters when they attempted to speak to the workers and collect information, photographs and video footage.
Earlier in the morning, Mohammad Amjad Hossain, superintendent of Gazipur Industrial Police, said a group of workers had attempted to block the Dhaka-Tangail highway in the Mouchak area of Kaliakair shortly before 8am.
Law enforcement personnel intervened and persuaded the workers to clear the road without confrontation, he said, adding that security forces remained on high alert at several points along the highway.

item.title: BGB deployment in Gazipur increased to 11 platoons, magistrates to 25
item.description:
The administration has strengthened security in Gazipur amid ongoing garment workers’ protests over wage increases and other demands, deploying an additional platoon of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel and increasing the number of executive magistrates.
The district now has 11 BGB platoons on duty, up from 10, while the number of executive magistrates has risen from 21 to 25.
Arif Hossain, assistant commissioner (media) at the Gazipur deputy commissioner’s office, confirmed the development on Tuesday morning.
He said BGB personnel were operating under the supervision of 25 executive magistrates, while other law enforcement agencies remained on high alert.
The additional deployment aims to prevent damage to public property and protect the lives and belongings of residents, he added.
Meanwhile, workers attempted to block the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur’s Mouchak area around 8:30am on Tuesday, but law enforcement personnel prevented them from occupying the road. Groups of workers were also seen heading to factories to join their shifts.
Mohammad Amjad Hossain, superintendent of Gazipur Industrial Police, said workers had attempted to block the highway shortly before 8am. Law enforcement personnel dispersed them, and traffic subsequently returned to normal.
For the past few days, garment workers in different parts of Gazipur have been staging protests over wage increases and other demands, blocking the Dhaka-Tangail and Dhaka-Mymensingh highways.
The unrest has involved incidents of arson, including fires at a police box, a police vehicle and a factory scrap warehouse. Clashes between workers and law enforcement personnel have also left people injured on both sides, while several individuals have been detained.
Several factories have suspended operations amid the protests.

item.title: Beyond equality: The unfinished journey of women's rights in Bangladesh
item.description:
Bangladesh's progress should be measured not only by economic growth, but by whether every woman and girl can live safely, learn, earn, speak and participate on equal terms.
A promise that must become everyday reality
Bangladesh has made important gains in girls' education and women's participation in public and economic life. Women work in factories, farms, schools, hospitals, businesses and public institutions; they support families and contribute to national development. Yet progress is not the same as equality. For many women, the ability to make choices about education, work, marriage, safety and public life is still constrained by violence, economic dependence and unequal expectations.
The Constitution provides a clear starting point. Articles 27 and 28 guarantee equality before the law and state that women have equal rights with men in all spheres of state and public life. The challenge is to make those guarantees real in homes, schools, workplaces, online spaces and public institutions.
The evidence on violence cannot be ignored
The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics and UNFPA's Violence Against Women Survey 2024, published in October 2025, found that 76 per cent of women had experienced at least one form of intimate-partner violence in their lifetime, while 49 per cent experienced it in the previous 12 months. The survey also found that many survivors do not disclose the violence they experience. These figures are not simply statistics: they represent barriers to safety, health, dignity and equal participation.
A survivor may remain silent because of fear, stigma, financial dependence, pressure to preserve a marriage, concern for children or a lack of confidence that help will be available. Responses must therefore go beyond asking women to report abuse. Police, health services, legal-aid providers, local government and community organisations need to offer confidential, accessible and survivor-centred support. Investigations must be timely, protection must be practical, and accountability must not depend on a woman's income or social influence.
A childhood should not be cut short
Child marriage is another barrier to equality. UNICEF's Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025 preliminary findings report that 47.2 per cent of women aged 20–24 were first married before age 18. Behind this measure are girls whose education may be interrupted and whose choices about health, work and family life can narrow before adulthood.
Preventing child marriage requires more than enforcement after a marriage has been arranged. Families need social protection and economic support; schools must be safe and accessible; girls need quality secondary education and trusted adults to turn to. Community leaders and local institutions should challenge the idea that early marriage is a solution to poverty or insecurity. A girl's future should not be treated as a family burden to be transferred through marriage.
Economic participation must mean real opportunity
Women's economic contribution is substantial, but opportunity remains unequal. The World Bank's Gender Data Portal, using ILO modelled estimates, reports that female labour-force participation in Bangladesh was 38.6 per cent in 2025, compared with 80.4 per cent for men. Labour-force figures do not capture the full value of unpaid care and household work, much of which is performed by women. They do, however, point to a significant gap in participation in paid work and economic activity.
Closing that gap requires safe transport, affordable childcare, fair recruitment and promotion, equal pay for work of equal value, maternity protection, skills training and access to finance. Women working in informal and home-based sectors also need stronger protections. Entrepreneurship programmes should provide more than motivational messages: women need markets, mentoring, digital access, credit on fair terms and control over the income they earn.
Representation is not the same as influence
Women must be able to shape decisions, not merely appear in photographs or occupy positions without authority. Political parties, local government bodies, trade unions, professional associations and public institutions should create transparent pathways for women to lead. That includes protection from harassment and intimidation, fair access to resources, and meaningful roles in policy development.
Young women in particular should be encouraged to participate in community decision-making and public debate. Their presence can broaden the questions institutions ask and the solutions they consider. But representation should be judged by whether women can speak freely, influence priorities and be held to the same standards of accountability as everyone else.
A shared responsibility
Women's rights are not a concern for women alone. Men and boys, families, educators, employers, journalists, religious and community leaders, and public officials all have a role in challenging discrimination. Equality begins in ordinary decisions: whether a daughter is encouraged to continue her studies, whether care work is shared at home, whether harassment is taken seriously, and whether a woman's opinion is respected.
Bangladesh needs measurable commitments: reduce child marriage; strengthen prevention and response to gender-based violence; improve access to justice and support services; expand safe and decent work; and ensure women's meaningful participation in leadership. Progress should be tracked with reliable data and public reporting, including attention to rural women, women with disabilities, low-income households and women facing overlapping forms of exclusion.
The measure of progress
The unfinished journey of women's rights is not about granting special privileges. It is about ensuring that rights already recognized in law can be exercised in daily life. A girl should be able to finish school without being pushed into marriage. A woman should be able to work without harassment, earn without discrimination and seek justice without fear. She should be able to take part in public life without being threatened or silenced.
Bangladesh's future will be stronger when women's safety, freedom and equal opportunity are treated not as optional development goals, but as foundations of national progress. Equality is not achieved when it is promised. It is achieved when women can experience it—in every home, workplace, classroom and institution.
Shejuti Hossain is a writer and human rights activist.

item.title: From climate pledges to youth power: Bangladesh’s opportunity ahead of COP31
item.description:
In 2019, a group of law students in the Pacific began asking whether governments could be held accountable under international law for their response to climate change. Six years later, in July 2025, the International Court of Justice issued an advisory opinion clarifying states’ climate obligations and responsibilities towards future generations. Young people had helped bring climate change before the world’s highest court.
Yet the money tells a different story. Between 2019 and 2021, youth-led climate justice initiatives received just 0.76% of mitigation-focused funding from some of the world’s largest climate foundations.
The contradiction is stark. Young people can influence international debates and national politics, yet struggle to secure the resources to turn their ideas into action. They are invited to conferences, consulted on policies and celebrated in public campaigns. But how much influence do they have over budgets, institutions and the decisions that determine where climate finance goes?
For Bangladesh, this is more than a question of representation. Generation Z played a defining role in reshaping Dhaka’s political landscape. As the country prepares for COP31, the challenge is to turn that civic influence into lasting institutional change.
Participation must lead to influence
Young people have spent years securing recognition within the UN climate process. YOUNGO, the official constituency for children and youth, gained full status in 2011. COP27 encouraged countries to include youth negotiators in national delegations, while COP28 established the Presidency Youth Climate Champion. At COP30 in Belém, youth consultations engaged thousands of participants.
These are worthwhile steps, but access does not guarantee influence. A conference badge cannot tell us whether young people changed a negotiating position, shaped a policy or influenced a budget. Travel costs, visa restrictions and limited observer places further disadvantage young people from least developed countries, small island developing states and climate-vulnerable communities.
The goal should be to connect participation with decisions, funding and measurable results.
Bangladesh has a foundation on which to build. Its National Adaptation Plan for 2023–2050 provides a long-term framework for climate resilience. Its NDC 3.0, submitted in 2025, includes child-sensitive targets for maintaining essential services during climate shocks. UNICEF has identified it as the first NDC globally to include youth in its measurement, reporting, and verification process.
The International Centre for Climate Change and Development (ICCCAD) at Independent University, Bangladesh, has also demonstrated what practical support can achieve. Between 2023 and 2026, its SIDA-supported CAP-RES project trained 100 youth fellows and funded 57 youth-led climate sub-projects, which together directly reached 47,795 people, nearly half of them women. Such experience shows the value of combining training, mentoring and funding with community-level action.
Still, engagement remains fragmented and often dependent on individual projects and donor support. Opportunities are concentrated in urban centres, while young people from coastal areas, haors, chars and hill districts face greater barriers. Indigenous youth, young women and persons with disabilities need more equitable access. The agenda must also extend beyond adaptation to clean energy, mitigation and green skills, which will shape future employment.
Why climate finance misses young people
The problem is not simply a shortage of money. It is also how funding is designed and distributed.
A review of 100 youth-focused climate finance initiatives by the Commonwealth Secretariat and YOUNGO, launched at COP28, found that funding was generally disbursed in small amounts and information about beneficiaries was often inadequate.
Young applicants may lack established financial systems, organisational experience or evidence of results. Funders, however, also impose complex application requirements and short funding periods that can exclude smaller organisations. Conventional lenders may consider early-stage youth enterprises too risky.
Not every climate initiative should be expected to generate revenue. Community adaptation, disaster preparedness and climate research deliver public benefits that may not produce commercial returns. They need grants and public funding, not debt. Concessional loans, guarantees and blended finance have a role where youth-led enterprises have credible business models and realistic repayment prospects.
International commitments provide an opportunity, but access remains a concern. At COP29, developed countries committed to take the lead in mobilising at least US$300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035, within a broader call to scale climate finance to US$1.3 trillion a year. COP30 called for adaptation finance to increase at least threefold by 2035.
For least developed countries, the terms matter as much as the headline figures. The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, for example, had around US$250 million available for its first call for proposals, against requests estimated at US$2 billion to US$3 billion.
Least developed countries have also committed, through the LDC Initiative for Effective Adaptation and Resilience, to channel 70% of climate finance to local-level action by 2030. Youth-led initiatives should be part of this effort, supported by accessible funding channels and proportionate accountability requirements.
Turning commitments into action
Bangladesh does not need an entirely new climate finance system. It needs to make existing institutions more accessible and accountable.
First, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should formalise youth representation in NDC 3.0 monitoring, National Adaptation Plan reviews, local climate planning and official COP delegations. Selection should be transparent and geographically representative. Institutions should report annually on which youth recommendations were adopted and explain why others were not.
Second, national financing institutions should establish accessible funding windows. Bangladesh Bank could assess how its young entrepreneurs and green finance mechanisms might support viable youth-led climate enterprises. The Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund, Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation and Infrastructure Development Company Limited should create dedicated funding windows or explicitly include eligible youth-led initiatives in existing programmes.
Third, funding must match purpose. Grants should support research, community adaptation, disaster preparedness and early-stage testing. Repayable finance should be reserved for enterprises with credible cash flows. Mentoring, financial-management support and safeguards against excessive debt should accompany funding, with clear pathways for successful pilots to access further grants, public programmes or investment.
Fourth, the Finance Division and environment ministry should introduce a youth marker in annual climate budget reporting. Development partners and national financing institutions should distinguish commitments from actual disbursements. A regularly updated national mapping of youth climate organisations would help identify funding gaps and measure progress.
Fifth, international climate funds should strengthen Enhanced Direct Access, giving accredited National Implementing Entities the resources and authority to establish locally managed youth grant mechanisms. Simplified procedures should be balanced with appropriate technical support and financial oversight.
Finally, Bangladesh and the LDCs Group should use COP31 to press for an adequately resourced Action for Climate Empowerment plan that strengthens young people’s influence over climate decisions. They should also advocate for more accessible finance for locally led climate action and loss and damage, linked to clear national responsibilities and follow-up.
The opportunity in Antalya
Representation without funding leaves young people unable to act. Funding without transparent selection can reinforce existing inequalities. Both require institutions that explain how youth contributions influence decisions and what funded initiatives achieve.
Ahead of COP31 in Antalya this November, Bangladesh has an opportunity to move beyond expressions of support towards measurable commitments: Formal youth representation, accessible financing and transparent reporting. Its experience in climate planning and locally led adaptation gives it a credible basis for making that case.
Generation Z, which helped bring climate change before the world’s highest court in the Pacific and played a defining role in reshaping Dhaka’s political landscape, does not need another pavilion or another invitation to speak. It needs the authority to influence policy, the resources to put ideas into practice, and the means to hold decision-makers accountable.
Giving young people a genuine share of responsibility is not a symbolic gesture. It is a practical investment in those who will live longest with the consequences of decisions made today.
------------------------------------------------------------
Arif M Faisal is the Director of ICCCAD at IUB. The views expressed herein are solely those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of any affiliated organization

item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has called for ensuring that young people’s innovative ideas are not left unrealised because of a lack of funding.
“A single innovative idea from you could prove to be a game-changer for Bangladesh,” he said, adding that the government had allocated Tk500 crore annually for startups in the current budget.
He made the remarks while addressing the inauguration of a two-day Solar Expo as the chief guest on Tuesday morning at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Exhibition Centre in Agargaon, Dhaka.
The exhibition, themed “Utilize every inch of your rooftop and increase income through solar energy,” opened to visitors immediately after the inaugural ceremony. The prime minister also toured various stalls.
Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Iqbal Hasan Mahmud presided over the event.
The prime minister said Bangladesh had previously become heavily dependent on imported energy, leaving the country vulnerable to disruptions in global supply chains caused by international conflicts.
To help stabilize the country's energy and power supply, the government had provided Tk43,000 crore in subsidies to the power sector in the 2025-26 fiscal year, he said.
He added that electricity demand remained at a similar level in the current fiscal year and that the government had increased its diesel reserves. Initiatives had also been taken to ensure adequate coal supplies for coal-fired power plants, while efforts to engage alternative suppliers were continuing.
The government had allocated Tk600 crore to procure fuel oil for electricity generation, he said.
Rather than spending time debating the failures or roles of previous governments in energy security and power generation, the government's priority was to meet future electricity demand and ensure an uninterrupted supply for households and businesses, he added.
He said the government was pursuing several initiatives simultaneously, including reviewing power-sector expenditure and contracts, intensifying domestic gas exploration, diversifying energy sources and rapidly expanding solar power generation.

item.title: Fresh clashes erupt as garment worker protests continue in Ashulia
item.description:
Ashulia’s industrial area remained tense on Tuesday as garment workers continued protesting for a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000, extending unrest that has persisted for several days.
Intermittent clashes between workers and police began around 9am at several points along the Baipail-Abdullahpur road and continued through the morning.
Workers had initially arrived at factories for their shifts. However, after 8:30am, several factories, including a Hamim Group facility in Narsinghapur, suspended operations, prompting workers to take to the streets.
As workers gathered outside factories and attempted to block roads, police fired tear gas shells to disperse them.
During the confrontations, protesters also set fires at several locations in an attempt to block the road.
As of 11:20am, the situation remained tense in Nishchintapur and the Unique area along the Baipail-Abdullahpur road.
Although police dispersed the protesters using tear gas and charges, workers later regrouped in nearby alleyways.
Sources said several factory authorities had been forced to suspend operations amid the unrest, but the exact number of affected factories was not immediately known.

item.title: US will stop $4b funding to Israel at end of 2026: Trump
item.description:
ISRAEL-PALESTINIANS-TRUMP-NETANYAHU

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion in funding to Israel after the end of this year.

Speaking to Fox News' Fox and Friends, Trump said Israel no longer needed the funding and that some Democrats and left-wing politicians were using the US financial support to Israel as a talking point to criticize Republicans.

"Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," Trump told Fox News' Fox and Friends.

"We've already agreed that by the end of this year we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it," he said.

There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu's office on Trump's remarks.

It was not immediately clear which exact funding Trump meant. A memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion annual US military aid to Israel is approaching its expiration date in 2028 and conversations have been under way on how Washington's assistance to Israel would evolve beyond that date.

"They can buy whatever they want. They can buy whatever they want. So can Europe. We make the greatest weapons in the world," Trump added on Tuesday.

Netanyahu said in a May interview with CBS that he hoped to wean Israel off US military support within a decade. In a June letter to a US congressman he wrote that the time had come for Israel "to move from aid recipient to partner."

US public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48 per cent of voters and 66 per cent of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16 per cent and 20 per cent when the question was first asked in 2017.

Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries and even moderate lawmakers are increasingly willing to challenge decades of US support for Israel.

"The left uses the $4 billion payment that everybody knows about, well it's no secret, as a signal of unfairness, and we can't allow that to happen," Trump said.

"We were giving them 4 billion, we are, but it gets cut off at the end of the year," he said. "Why? Because they don't need it."

item.title: ‘I am a poor man’s son, I could not resist the temptation of money’: ‘Coordinator’ Riyad
item.description:
First, they raided the house of former member of parliament (MP) Shammi Ahmed with the police. After failing to find her, the police left. But the men returned to the house shortly afterwards and threatened to have her husband arrested, branding him an ‘Awami League collaborator’. They demanded Tk 5 million in extortion money, of which the self-proclaimed ‘coordinators’ managed to collect Tk 1 million. A few days later, five of them were caught by police when they returned to collect the remaining Tk 4 million. Another suspect was arrested subsequently.

The Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) has submitted a charge sheet against six people before the court after completing its investigation into the case filed over the incident in Gulshan.

According to the PBI investigation, following the political changeover on 5 August, the accused began identifying themselves as coordinators and active members of the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement. Taking advantage of this identity, they regularly visited police stations and developed close ties with police officers by offering assistance in arresting leaders and activists affiliated with the Awami League who were accused in various cases, as well as providing information about their whereabouts.

The investigation found that the accused subsequently used this access to evade the attention of law enforcement agencies and identify various individuals as Awami League collaborators, associates or supporters. They allegedly demanded and collected money by threatening them with cases, arrest and harassment. Through these activities, the accused exploited their influence for personal gain and obtained illegal financial benefits.

In the charge sheet, investigating officer Firoz Ahmed Munshi stated that the investigation and evidence had established the offences under Sections 143, 448, 385 and 386 of the Penal Code against Abdur Razzak alias Riyad and Jane Alam Apu. Meanwhile, preliminary evidence had established offences under Sections 143, 448 and 385 against the other accused, Sakadoun Siam, Sadman Sadab and Ibrahim Hossain.

The case was filed at Gulshan Police Station on 27 July 2025 by Siddiq Abu Zafar, 75. He lives in a house on Road 83 in Gulshan-2. According to the investigation records, his wife is former MP Shammi Ahmed.

Initially, Sub-Inspector (SI) Mokhlesur Rahman of Gulshan Police Station investigated the case. The PBI subsequently took over the investigation. Its SI Firoz Ahmed Munshi submitted the charge sheet against six people on 15 October after completing the investigation.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, he said, “As one of the accused is a minor, he will be tried in the juvenile court. The next hearing in the case is scheduled for 10 November. The court will hear arguments on whether to accept the charge sheet that day. All six accused in the case are currently out on bail.”

However, a check with the general registration (GR) section of the police station on 1 November found that the charge sheet had not yet been submitted to the court.

Money demanded by threatening arrest

According to the PBI investigation, on the night of 16 July 2025, several people identifying themselves as coordinators of the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement gathered at the Gulshan-2 roundabout after receiving information that Shammi Ahmed was at her Gulshan residence.

Later, at around 2am, Abdur Razzak and Jane Alam Apu went to Gulshan Police Station, informed the police about the matter and asked them to arrange a raid to arrest her.

The police station informed the deputy commissioner of police of the Gulshan Division. Subsequently, a team comprising police officers and the self-proclaimed coordinators went to the house.

Citing information obtained during the investigation and an examination of video footage, the PBI said that in the early hours of 17 July, several police personnel led by Gulshan Police Station SI Arman Ali, along with Abdur Razzak, Jane Alam Apu, Sakadoun Siam, Sadman Sadab, Ibrahim Hossain, Aminul Islam and 10 to 12 others, went to the residence. Identifying themselves as coordinators, they searched different rooms for the former MP.

Failing to find Shammi Ahmed, they prepared a search list at around 6:30am and left the house.

However, shortly after the police left, Abdur Razzak and Jane Alam Apu returned to the residence. According to the PBI investigation records, they branded the complainant an Awami League collaborator and threatened to have him arrested. They demanded Tk 5 million to spare him from arrest.

Intimidated by the threats, the complainant agreed to pay. After receiving Tk 1 million immediately, the accused left, asking him to keep the remaining Tk 4 million ready. The investigation records also mention that investigators obtained video footage of the money being handed over.

Later, at around 10:30pm on 19 July, Abdur Razzak and Jane Alam Apu returned to the residence. They knocked repeatedly on the flat's door, but left when nobody opened it.

The PBI said an examination of call detail records (CDRs) subsequently confirmed their presence at the scene at that time.

Arrested while collecting the remaining money

According to the PBI investigation records, the accused returned to the house at around 5:30pm on 26 July to collect the remaining Tk 4 million.

The complainant was not at home at the time. Mohammad Hannan, a security guard at the residence, informed him over the phone. The complainant immediately alerted Gulshan Police Station.

Police quickly arrived at the scene and detained Abdur Razzak, Sakadoun Siam, Sadman Sadab, Ibrahim Hossain and Aminul Islam, who was a minor. Jane Alam Apu managed to flee. He was subsequently arrested with the assistance of the Detective Branch (DB) of police.

Among the six arrested, Abdur Razzak and Jane Alam Apu gave confessional statements before the court under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The investigation records state that both admitted to receiving the money in their statements.

‘I could not resist the temptation of money’

In his statement before the court, Abdur Razzak alias Riyad admitted to receiving the extortion money.

In the statement, he identified himself as the acting convener of the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement among students at a private university. He also claimed to have assisted the police on several occasions in arresting people he described as ‘fascist elements’.

According to Riyad's statement, after receiving information that Shammi Ahmed was at her Gulshan residence on the night of 17 July 2025, they went to the police station. A police team subsequently accompanied them to raid the house. Shammi was not found there.

Riyad told the court that while returning from the house, Jane Alam Apu had brought an AirPod device with him. The device had the words ‘Shammi AirPod’ written on it. They returned to the house at around 10am to hand it back.

Apu entered the house on the pretext of drinking water. They then told the complainant that they knew his wife was inside the house and that they would hand her over to the police.

When the complainant agreed to pay, they initially demanded Tk 5 million. The complainant offered Tk 1 million, which they accepted. They later took the money to Riyad's house and divided it equally among themselves.

Regarding the attempt to collect the remaining Tk 4 million, Riyad said he sent Ibrahim Hossain, Sakadoun Siam and Sadman Sadab to the house at around 5pm on 26 July.

According to him, the police asked him to go to the house as part of a plan to trap him. He was then at the roundabout. Believing what the police told him, he went to the scene. The complainant alerted the police, who arrived and caught them red-handed.

At the end of his statement, Riyad said, “I am a poor man's son. I could not resist the temptation of money. I apologise.”

Apu bought a motorcycle with the extortion money

The investigation records state that accused Jane Alam Apu also admitted to receiving the money in his statement before the court. However, he claimed that he was not present at the scene when the accused demanded the remaining Tk 4 million.

The PBI, however, said Apu was present at the scene but fled.

According to Apu's statement, he had previously served as a coordinator of a committee. On the night of 17 July, after receiving information in a WhatsApp group that a former female MP was at a residence in Gulshan, he went there. A police team subsequently accompanied them to raid the house. The former MP was not found during the raid.

Apu said, “After that, Riyad took me to the house again. When we demanded money from the complainant, he initially agreed to pay Tk 500,000. But Riyad demanded Tk 10 million. After lengthy negotiations, the amount was settled at Tk 5 million. He then gave us Tk 1 million.”

According to Apu, they took the money to Riyad's house in Badda and divided it equally, receiving Tk 500,000 each.

He said he spent Tk 307,000 from his share to buy a Yamaha FZ-X motorcycle and used some of the money to repay debts. He also claimed that an attempt to send another Tk 50,000 through bKash went to the wrong number.

Later, Tk 17,000 was recovered from him.

Apu claimed that when Riyad called him to collect the remaining Tk 4 million, he refused to go. He subsequently cut off contact with Riyad.

He maintained that although Riyad later went to the house with others to demand the money, he was not there and had not exerted any pressure on the former female MP.

Motorcycle and iPhones seized

According to the investigation records, Tk 298,000 and two mobile phones were seized from a house in the Baitakali area of East Badda, identified by Abdur Razzak. The seized phones included a Redmi Note 10 Pro and two iPhone 13 devices.

Meanwhile, acting on information provided by Jane Alam Apu, police seized a Yamaha FZ-X motorcycle, an iPhone 11 and Tk 17,000 in cash from a garage at a house in the Nabinagar area of Mohammadpur.

Akram Hossain, lawyer for the main accused in the case, Abdur Razzak Riyad, told Prothom Alo, “We have not seen the charge sheet yet. We will file a petition in court on behalf of Riyad.”

Attempts to contact Abdur Razzak Riyad, the main accused who is currently out on bail, for his comments on the charge sheet were unsuccessful.

When his phone number was contacted, it was found that his elder brother, Rezaul Karim, was now using it. Riyad's elder brother, Mohammad Rezaul Karim, said Riyad did not wish to comment on the case at this stage.

Expectation of maximum punishment

Muhammad Shamsuddoha Sumon, additional public prosecutor at the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court, told Prothom Alo that Abdur Razzak Riyad, who introduced himself as a leader of the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement, was the mastermind behind the extortion.

“He was remanded by the court several times during that period. Everyone accused in the extortion case has been included in the charge sheet. They will face trial in accordance with the charges, and we will seek the maximum punishment for them,” he said.

Zahurul Alam, lawyer for the complainant Siddiq Abu Zafar, told Prothom Alo that he was satisfied that the investigating officer had submitted the charge sheet under the relevant legal provisions. He said they wanted justice.

item.title: Home Ministry asked to take control of properties owned by Sheikh Hasina, Asaduzzaman
item.description:
The Chief Prosecutor's Office has sent a letter to the Ministry of Home Affairs to take control of all movable and immovable properties of the ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and former Home Minister Asaduzzaman Khan, who have been convicted of crimes against humanity.

Chief Prosecutor Md Aminul Islam confirmed to Prothom Alo that the letter was sent today, Tuesday.

The Registrar of the International Crimes Tribunal, the Personal Secretary to the Home Minister, and the Personal Secretary to the Law Minister have been informed about the letter signed by the Chief Prosecutor.

The subject of the letter relates to the implementation of the order to confiscate the properties of the fugitive convicts Sheikh Hasina and Asaduzzaman Khan, who were sentenced by the International Crimes Tribunal-1.

According to the letter, on 17 November 2025, Tribunal-1 sentenced Sheikh Hasina and Asaduzzaman Khan to death for crimes against humanity.

The order was given to seize all properties of the two convicts to distribute compensation to the families of the martyrs and victims of the July uprising.

The tribunal instructed the Ministry of Home Affairs to take necessary measures to implement the property seizure order.

The letter from the Chief Prosecutor's Office further states that if the government does not immediately take control of all movable and immovable properties of the convicted fugitives Sheikh Hasina and Asaduzzaman Khan, they may dispose of, sell, or otherwise transfer the properties at any time, rendering the tribunal's confiscation-related verdict and order ineffective.

In such a situation, it is urgently requested to prepare a complete list of all movable and immovable properties of Sheikh Hasina and Asaduzzaman Khan, take control of them by the state, and distribute them as compensation to the families of the martyrs and victims of the July uprising as per the tribunal's order.

What assets does Sheikh Hasina have?

As candidates in the 2024 twelfth national parliamentary election, Sheikh Hasina (Gopalganj-3) and Asaduzzaman Khan Kamal (Dhaka-12) submitted affidavits. From these, their declared asset information can be known.
In the affidavit, Awami League President Sheikh Hasina reported immovable and movable assets valued at Tk 43.4 million under her name.

At that time, she showed cash of Tk 28,500. The amount deposited in banks and financial institutions was about Tk 23.9 million. There were savings certificates worth Tk 2.5 million and fixed deposits (FDR) worth Tk 5.5 million.

Sheikh Hasina declared three motor vehicles in the affidavit, one of which was a gift. She did not declare its value. The remaining two were valued at Tk 4.7 million. Gold and other precious metals were valued at Tk 1. 325 million. She declared the value of her furniture at Tk 740,000.

Sheikh Hasina declared 15. 3 bighas of agricultural land in her name, with a purchased portion valued at Tk 678,000, located in Tungipara, Gopalganj Sadar, Gazipur, and Rangpur.

There is a family farmhouse of Sheikh Hasina and her family located in Telirchala, Mouja, 13 kilometers from Gazipur city, adjacent to the Dhaka-Tangail highway, near the Bangladesh Scout Training Centre.

According to local land office sources, around 1970, a local individual had written this land in the name of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.

Sheikh Hasina and Sheikh Rehana inherited ownership of the land. Later, Sheikh Hasina and Sheikh Rehana transferred parts of the land to their children. Consequently, Sheikh Hasina's children Sajib Wazed and Saima Wazed and Sheikh Rehana's children Radwan Mujib Siddiq and Azmina Siddiq became owners. Documents show the land amounting to 297 decimal (9 bighas).

According to the affidavit, Sheikh Hasina has a plot in Purbachal, Dhaka, valued at Tk 3.476 million.

While serving as Prime Minister, Sheikh Hasina, her son Sajib Wazed, daughter Saima Wazed, younger sister Sheikh Rehana (Rehana Siddiq), Rehana's son Radwan Mujib Siddiq, and daughter Azmina Siddiq (Rooponti) were each allotted 10 kathas of land in Purbachal.

In total, the six family members received 60 kathas of land. Allegations of abuse of power and irregularities in these allocations led to ongoing cases by the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC).

In the affidavit, Sheikh Hasina showed a three-story building with 6.10 decimals (partially) of land in her name. This land is in Tungipara, Gopalganj. The value during acquisition is shown as Tk 500,000.

On 22 May of last year, the ACC stated in a briefing that Sheikh Hasina had provided false information on her asset disclosure affidavit during the 2008 ninth national parliamentary elections. At the time, she declared having 6.50 acres of land in her name. The purchase price was shown as Tk 175,000.

The ACC revealed that upon verification at the time, Sheikh Hasina had more than 28.41 acres of immovable property in her name. Consequently, the ACC sent a letter to the Election Commission to address the issue.

According to land office sources, the ownership of the house at Dhanmondi 32 belongs to the Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Memorial Trust.

Sheikh Hasina's residence, Sudha Sadan, in Dhanmondi, belongs to Sajib Wazed and Saima Wazed.

Asaduzzaman Khan's assets

Former Home Minister Asaduzzaman Khan participated in elections from Dhaka-12 constituency and became a member of parliament. The affidavit he submitted for the twelfth national parliamentary election provides information on declared immovable and movable properties.

Asaduzzaman Khan declared having more than Tk 8.4 million in cash. He showed Tk 8.2 million in bank and financial institution deposits. There were bonds and shares worth about Tk 2.4 million. Postal savings certificates or fixed deposits were shown at Tk 20.1 million.

Asaduzzaman Khan valued two motor vehicles at Tk 16.1 million. His electronic equipment and furniture were valued at Tk 200,000.

He showed a business capital loan of Tk 22 million. He declared 10 tolas of gold, though the price was not mentioned.

According to the affidavit, Asaduzzaman Khan has 171 decimals (over 5 bighas) of agricultural land, valued at Tk 10. 6 million at acquisition.

He has 18. 5 decimals of non-agricultural land, valued at Tk 5.8 million at acquisition. He declared the value of two properties in house and apartment columns. One is noted as a village house, valued at Tk 8 million at acquisition. The other was valued at around Tk 1. 3 million.

Altogether, Asaduzzaman Khan's assets are valued at approximately Tk 102. 5 million (excluding the value of 10 tolas of gold).

The ACC is also investigating Asaduzzaman Khan's assets.

ACC officials have stated that he owns assets beyond known income. The ACC has filed a case in this regard. It was stated in court that he acquired and possessed ownership of asset-value inconsistencies amounting to Tk 164. 2 million through dishonest means.

item.title: Garment workers’ wage board: No step to call meeting in 3 days
item.description:
The government formed a minimum wage board last Sunday to increase wages for workers in the ready-made garment (RMG) industry.

Two days have already passed, but no initiative has been taken to arrange the first meeting of the wage board.

Meanwhile, protests and clashes between workers and police continued today, Tuesday, in Gazipur, Savar-Ashulia and Mirpur.

The Ministry of Labour reconstituted the minimum wage board through a notification on Sunday.

Dhaka University Professor Mosleh Uddin Ahmed was appointed as the independent member of the board, while Asif Ayub, joint secretary general of the Bangladesh Employers' Federation, and Anwar Hossain, president of the Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal, were appointed as the permanent members representing the owners and workers, respectively.

Another gazette was issued on the same day, appointing ABM Shamsuddin, a director of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), as the representative of the owners and Babul Akhtar, general secretary of the Bangladesh Garment and Industrial Workers Federation (BGIWF), as the representative of the workers on the minimum wage board formed for the RMG industry.

The six-member wage board will work for the RMG industry with Senior District and Sessions Judge Sheikh Ashfaqur Rahman as its chairman.

Asked when the first meeting of the wage board would be held, its chairman, Senior District and Sessions Judge Sheikh Ashfaqur Rahman, told Prothom Alo on Tuesday afternoon, “We will hold a meeting of the wage board soon. We are ready to hold the meeting.”

Sheikh Ashfaqur Rahman said the first meeting of the previous wage board was held 45 days after the notification was issued. The entire process was completed in six to seven months. This time, however, it would not be the same. The government is sincere about completing the process of determining wages within a short time.

The two representatives of the workers on the wage board, Anwar Hossain and Babul Akhtar, held a press conference at the Shram Bhaban yesterday, Monday, urging that a meeting of the wage board be called as soon as possible. They said they would write to the board chairman in this regard.

At the press conference, Babul Akhtar said, “The latest minimum wage structure came into effect in December 2023. Accordingly, a new wage structure is due next December. We will work in such a way that workers receive their wages in January. There is no reason for any delay on our part. If necessary, we will hold meetings of the wage board consecutively. We have no objection to holding meetings throughout the night. We will make no compromise in ensuring workers' rightful wages.”

The last minimum wage board for the RMG industry was formed in 2023. The wage structure was legally required to come into effect on 1 December that year. On 9 April, the Ministry of Labour appointed representatives of the owners and workers to the wage board. The board held six meetings and recommended a minimum wage of Tk 12,500 in the first week of November. The government issued the final notification in December.

The government first formed a minimum wage board for RMG workers in 1994. That board set the minimum wage at Tk 930. In 2006, it was increased to Tk 1,662.50. The 2010 wage board set the minimum wage for workers at Tk 3,000. The 2013 wage board determined the minimum wage at Tk 5,300. The 2018 wage board finalised the minimum wage for garment workers at Tk 8,000.

item.title: Dwip tactfully avoids questions, police seek fresh remand
item.description:
In the murder case of former Bangladesh Air Force Flight Lieutenant KM Tahsif Sauri, the police want to take Ahmed Shahriar Reza Dwip, referred to as a ''younger brother-like friend'', into remand for questioning for the second time.

A seven-day remand request has been made for this purpose.

In the application for the second remand of Dwip, the investigation officer of the case stated that during the first round of remand questioning, the accused provided some important information about the incident.

These pieces of information are being verified. The accused is of a very cunning nature, and hence he tactfully avoids answering multiple questions during interrogation and maintains silence. To question him intensively, it is necessary to take him back into remand.

Tahsif murder case: ‘Younger friend’ Dwip placed on 4-day remand

The investigation officer of the case, Inspector Firoz Uddin of the Naval Police’s Tongi Outpost, applied for this remand in the Dhaka court today, Tuesday.

Public prosecutor Shamsuddoha Sumon confirmed this information to Prothom Alo.

Shamsuddoha Sumon mentioned that the hearing on this remand application is supposed to occur today, Tuesday in the court of Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Hasan Shahadat.

Following his arrest in the case, Dwip was taken into custody for a four-day remand last Saturday for questioning. Today, the Naval Police again applied for his remand for further questioning. In the same case, a young woman, who has also been arrested, is under a four-day remand. Her remand was granted last Sunday.

Ex-Air Force officer’s body recovered from Turag River

On the evening of 27 October, Tahsif went missing after leaving home following Dwip's call. The next afternoon, his body was recovered by the Naval Police from the area of Rajabari Ghat on the Turag River.

In connection with Tahsif's death, his father KM Enayetul Karim filed a murder case last Friday night at the Uttar Khan Police Station in the capital, naming unidentified individuals as the accused.
